newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba's Meister-stability orientation key for Euro.
newsitem.headline: Buba's Meister-stability orientation key for Euro.

text.p: Bundesbank directorate member Edgar Meister said on Monday the success of Europe's common currency largely depended on a stability-oriented interpretation of the entry criteria for EMU.

Adding his voice to the raging debate on what Europe's planned currency union might look like and when it might actually begin, Meister took an uncompromising tone on the importance of the various entry criteria.

"In order to keep dangers to integration low even in the runup to currency union, it is important to insist on a stability-oriented interpretation of the fiscal criteria put down in the Maastricht Treaty," Meister said.
The Bundesbank made a copy of the speech, delivered in Vienna, available in Frankfurt.

Such a strict interpretation would lead to a "homongenous but also small number of nations reaching the third stage of currency union, and this would be a key precondition for the euro to be a stable currency," Meister said.

Budget developments in Europe remained a source of concern particularly as the government debt ratio to gross domestic product, which the Maastricht Treaty says must be around a reference value of 60 percent, is far above 70 percent in a number of nations, Meister said.

Even Germany, once the prize pupil in Europe, is having trouble meeting the fiscal criteria, Meister said, noting that it was still too early to say with any certainty whether Germany would meet the deficit goal precisely.
"Much will depend on the forecast for tax revenues expected in May of this year," Meister explained.
The Maastricht Treaty says that nations' budget deficits should be near a reference value of three percent to gross domestic product.

German government officials have predicted the 1997 deficit would be at 2.9 percent, but independent economists fear the number will top some 3.4 percent in light of Germany's record unemployment levels.
Nonetheless, Meister said he is confident that the currency union would begin on time in 1999 and that Austria would be among the first group of nations to enter the union.

Meister said a stability-oriented interpretation of the Maastricht Treaty criteria is essential so that the future European central bank gets off to a successful start and some of a currency union's benefits become apparent.

"Especially at the beginning it is particularly important for the future european central bank to take care to create trust and recognition, the bank must see that a common European stability culture is created," Meister said.

Meister's comments stood in some contrast to comments made by his colleague Ernst Welteke, head of the state central bank in Hesse, who last Monday said Germany would likely miss the deficit goal but that this should not not be excluded from being among the first nations to join the currency union.

Meister said it was imperative that restructuring programmes already launched must now be maintained, warning that accounting tricks or one-off efforts to try and squeeze budgets into the set parameters for currency union, was not a wise idea.
"Accounting tricks, which push a part of the deficit into the future, and one-off effects would not build a solid base for decisions for the currency union," Meister said.

Recently a number of nations -- including France and Italy -- have drawn on a variety of special measures, including a one-off tax and shifting some pension funds, to help whip their budgets into shape. While the measures were decreed to be legal, German policy makers have viewed these critically.
Meister also warned that the temptation to use creative bookkeeping tactics may increase if the stability pact, agreed to at the summit in Dublin last December, were watered down in any way.
"The less there remains of the original ideas of a stability pact and its automatic sanctions, the greater the temptation to use the the aforementioned 'creative bookkeeping' methods," Meister said.
On the other hand Meister warned that the euro would not be a panacea to Europe's problems, including high unemployment levels.
"Even the expected recovery in economic growth this year will not be able to create a deep improvement on the labour market in the short-term," Meister said.
Before the currency union begins, Meister said there was still much work to be done, especially on the technical side.

The issue of minimum reserves, which has been very important to German policy makers, is also being discussed and Meister said, "I view the chances to be good that the European central bank will actually implement the instrument." Meister argued the instrument helps stabilise money market rates.
--Svea Herbst-Bayliss, Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525
